idiom_name: std::function<Step()> thunks driven by a while loop
implementation_notes: Hand-rolled in modern C++: a step is a std::function returning the next Step, and std::optional<T> marks the finished case, so the driver is `while (step.more) step = step.more(); return *step.value;`. Capturing by value inside the thunk keeps the state alive after the producing frame has returned; the alternative std::variant<T, std::function<Step()>> form removes the need for two fields and lets std::visit dispatch the step. Keep this shape only where depth is data-driven - a bounded recursion is better left as an ordinary function - and prefer the C++20 coroutine realization where the toolchain allows it.
pitfalls: A thunk that captures by reference dangles as soon as the producing frame returns; capture by value or keep the state in a shared_ptr.
std::function allocates whenever the capture exceeds its small buffer, so one heap allocation per step is the normal cost; std::variant step types avoid it where the step set is closed.
Leaving one edge of the mutual group uncalled-through reintroduces stack growth on exactly that edge.

variants.name: C++20 coroutine chain with symmetric transfer
variants.idiom_name: co_await / symmetric transfer instead of hand-written thunks
variants.implementation_notes: With C++20 coroutines the driver loop disappears into the coroutine machinery: the task awaiter returns the successor coroutine handle from await_suspend, so resuming the next coroutine unwinds the current frame first and the number of stack frames never grows (Baker, 2020, on symmetric transfer). This is the modern replacement for hand-written thunk loops in library-grade code; keep the std::function form when the standard is older than C++20, when the step must stay an inspectable value, or when a coroutine frame per step would be heavier than the recursion it replaces.
pitfalls: Asymmetric resume-from-inside-a-coroutine still nests frames: the awaiter must transfer by returning a handle, not by calling resume().
Detached coroutines must own their state; a frame referring to somebody else's destroyed object is the coroutine-era dangling-capture bug.
Coroutine frames are heap-allocated by default, so a step that was a cheap closure becomes an allocation plus type-erasure.
